title: The C++ string class
overview: Module 5 replaces char arrays with `std::string`. You assign and compare with ordinary operators, read characters safely, change strings with built-in modifiers, walk them with iterators, read whole lines with `getline`, and split lines into words with `stringstream`.

concepts.explain: `string` grows by itself and supports `=`, `==`, `+`; char arrays need `strcpy`/`strcmp`.
`begin()` is the first element, `end()` is one past the last.
concepts.snippet: for (auto it = s.begin(); it != s.end(); it++) cout << *it;

concepts.explain: `getline(cin, s)` reads a whole line into a string.
Turns a string into an input stream so `>>` can split it into words.

files.title: C strings vs the string class
files.what: Shows that `string` can be assigned with `=` and compared with `==`, while C char arrays need `strcpy` and `strcmp`.
steps: `string s = "hello"; s = "world";` just works.
`r == r2` compares the text of two strings.
A string can be given a longer value at any time - it grows by itself.

check.q: What C function does `r == r2` replace?

files.title: Accessing characters: [], at, front, back
files.what: Reads one word and prints its first and last characters in different ways.
steps: `s[0]` and `s.at(0)` both give the first character (`at` also checks the index).
`s.back()` and `s[s.size()-1]` give the last character.
`s.front()` is another way to get the first.
files.output_note: For `Phitron`: the first character is `P` (three ways) and the last is `n` (two ways).

check.q: What is the difference between `s[10]` and `s.at(10)` on a short string?
check.a: `s[10]` is undefined behaviour; `s.at(10)` throws an `out_of_range` exception.

files.title: size, capacity, clear, empty, resize
steps: `s.size()` is the number of characters (5 for Hello).
`s.max_size()` is the theoretical limit; `s.capacity()` is the room already reserved.
`s.clear()` empties the text but keeps the capacity.
`s.empty()` checks for length 0.
`s.resize(n)` cuts or pads; `resize(n, 'x')` pads with `x`.
files.output_note: Size `5`, a huge max size, capacity `15` (GCC keeps 15 characters inside the object). After `clear()` size is 0 but capacity is still 15. `resize(10)` gives `I would li`; `resize(15)` pads with invisible null characters; `resize(15, 'x')` gives `I would lixxxxx`.

files.title: Modifying strings
steps: `s += s2` and `s.append(...)` add text at the end.
`s.insert(5, " C++ ")` puts text at index 5.
`push_back('!')` adds one char; `pop_back()` removes the last.
`assign` works like `=`.
`erase(5)` keeps only the first 5 chars; `erase(1, 2)` removes 2 chars from index 1.
`replace(6, 5, X)` swaps 5 chars at index 6 for X; with length 0 it just inserts.
files.output_note: Follow `s`: `Hello world, Hi there` -> insert gives `Hello C++  world, Hi there` -> `s[0]='K'` makes it `Kello...` -> `erase(5)` gives `Kello` -> `erase(1, 2)` gives `Klo`. `s4` becomes `Hello Bangladesh`, then `Hello BangladeshBangladesh`.
files.watch_out: The line after `s[0] = 'K'` prints `s2` (still `Rahim`) although the label talks about the change; the change is to `s`, which you only see in the pop_back line.

files.title: Iterators: begin() and end()
files.what: `begin()` points at the first character and `end()` points one past the last. Loops can walk a string with an iterator or with `auto`.
steps: Print each character with an index loop.
`*s.begin()` is `H`; `*(s.end()-1)` is the last character `!`.
`string::iterator it` walks from `begin()` to `end()`, printing `*it`.
The same loop with `auto it` is shorter.
files.output_note: Line 2 ends with `H` because the index loop has no newline before `*s.begin()`. The next line looks blank: it is `*s.end()`. Then `!`, and two columns of letters from the two iterator loops.
files.watch_out: `*s.end()` is undefined behaviour; it happens to print the hidden null character here. Only dereference `end() - 1`.

check.a: None - it points one past the last character, so it must not be dereferenced.

files.title: getline for strings
files.what: `getline(cin, s)` reads a whole line into a `string`. After reading a number, `cin.ignore()` is needed before the next `getline`.
steps: `getline(cin, s)` reads the first line.
`cin >> x` reads a number.
`cin.ignore()` removes the newline.
`getline(cin, s2)` reads the next full line.
files.input:
Learning C++ strings
25
Bangladesh is beautiful
files.input_note: A line, a number, then another line.
files.output_note: The first line, `25`, then `Bangladesh is beautiful` - both lines kept their spaces.

check.a: The first reads into a `string` (no size limit); the second reads into a char array.

files.title: Splitting words with stringstream
files.what: Wraps a line in a `stringstream` so `>>` can pull out one word at a time; used to split lines and count words.
steps: `stringstream ss(s)` makes a stream from the line.
Each `ss >> word` takes the next word.
`while (ss2 >> word)` prints every word of line 2.
The third loop also counts the words.
files.input:
I love to code daily
big brown fox
  one two   three four
files.input_note: Three lines of words (the third has extra spaces).
files.output_note: First four words `I`, `love`, `to`, `code` (the fourth label wrongly says "third"). Then `big`, `brown`, `fox`. The third line gives four words and the count `4` - extra spaces are ignored.
files.watch_out: The fourth print is labelled "third word" by mistake.

check.q: Why does the count ignore the extra spaces?
check.a: `>>` skips any whitespace before each word.

recap: `end()` is one past the last character - never dereference it.
`stringstream` + `while (ss >> w)` splits a line into words.

check_yourself.a: Removes everything from index 3 to the end.

check_yourself.q: How do you count words in a line that may have several spaces between words?
check_yourself.a: Put the line in a `stringstream` and count how many times `ss >> word` succeeds.

check_yourself.q: What is the difference between `size()` and `capacity()`?
check_yourself.a: `size()` is the number of characters stored; `capacity()` is how many fit before the string must grow.
